subject: Social Science
question_english: How is groundwater being overused in India?
question_hinglish: India mein bhoojal ka zyada use kaise ho raha hai?
answer_english: Groundwater is under serious threat of overuse. About 300 districts reported a water level decline of over 4 metres in 20 years, and nearly one-third of the country overuses its groundwater; in 25 years, 60 per cent could be doing the same. Overuse is high in prosperous Punjab and western UP, hard-rock plateaus of central and south India, some coastal areas and growing cities. Groundwater is renewable, but using more than rain replenishes amounts to overuse.
answer_hinglish: Bhoojal ke zyada use ka gambhir khatra hai. Lagbhag 300 districts mein 20 saal mein paani ka star 4 metre se zyada gira, aur desh ka lagbhag ek-tihaai bhoojal zyada use kar raha hai; 25 saal mein 60 percent aisa kar sakta hai. Zyada use samriddh Punjab aur western UP, central aur south India ke kathor chattaani pathaaron, kuch tatiya ilaakon aur badhte shehron mein hai. Bhoojal renewable hai, par baarish se jitna bharta hai usse zyada lena zyada use hai.
ncert_context: Recent evidence suggests groundwater is under serious threat of overuse in many parts of the country. About 300 districts have reported a water level decline of over 4 metres during the past 20 years. Nearly one-third of the country is overusing their groundwater reserves. Groundwater overuse is particularly found in the agriculturally prosperous regions of Punjab and Western U.P., hard rock plateau areas of central and south India, some coastal areas and rapidly growing urban settlements. Groundwater is a renewable resource, replenished by nature, but if we use more than what is replenished by rain we would be overusing it.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Show with examples how the three sectors are interdependent.
question_hinglish: Examples ke saath dikhao ki teeno sectors ek-doosre pe kaise nirbhar hain.
answer_english: If farmers refuse to sell sugarcane to a mill, the mill must shut down, showing industry depends on agriculture. If companies stop buying Indian cotton, cotton prices fall and farmers may go bankrupt, showing agriculture depends on industry. If fertiliser or pumpset prices rise, farmers' costs rise and profits fall. If transporters strike, food becomes scarce in cities while farmers cannot sell their produce, showing dependence on the tertiary sector.
answer_hinglish: Agar kisan sugar mill ko ganna bechna band karein toh mill band ho jaayegi, yaani udyog kheti pe nirbhar hai. Agar companies Indian cotton khareedna band karein toh cotton ke daam girenge aur kisan diwaaliya ho sakte hain, yaani kheti udyog pe nirbhar hai. Agar fertiliser ya pumpset ke daam badhein toh kisaanon ki laagat badhegi aur munaafa ghatega. Agar transporters hadtaal karein toh shehron mein khaane ki kami hogi aur kisan apna maal nahi bech paayenge, jo tertiary sector pe nirbharta dikhata hai.
ncert_context: Imagine what would happen if farmers refuse to sell sugarcane to a sugar mill. The mill will have to shut down; this shows the secondary sector depends on the primary. If companies decide not to buy from the Indian market and import all cotton, Indian cotton cultivation will become less profitable and farmers may go bankrupt; cotton prices will fall. Farmers buy tractors, pumpsets, electricity, pesticides and fertilisers; if prices of fertilisers or pumpsets go up, cost of cultivation will rise and profits will be reduced. If there is a strike by transporters and lorries refuse to take vegetables and milk from rural areas, food will become scarce in urban areas whereas farmers will be unable to sell. Economic activities are highly interdependent.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Why are only final goods and services counted while calculating GDP?
question_hinglish: GDP nikaalte waqt sirf final goods aur services hi kyun gine jaate hain?
answer_english: Intermediate goods, like wheat and flour, are used up in producing final goods, like biscuits that reach consumers. The value of final goods already includes the value of all intermediate goods used to make them; for example, biscuits worth ₹80 already include the flour worth ₹25. Counting wheat, flour and biscuits separately would count the same value several times, so only final goods and services are counted.
answer_hinglish: Gehun aur aata jaise intermediate goods final goods, jaise consumers tak pahunchne wale biscuits, banane mein khap jaate hain. Final goods ki keemat mein un saare intermediate goods ki keemat pehle se shaamil hoti hai; jaise ₹80 ke biscuits mein ₹25 ka aata shaamil hai. Gehun, aata aur biscuits alag-alag ginne se ek hi keemat kai baar gini jaayegi, isliye sirf final goods aur services gine jaate hain.
ncert_context: Not every good that is produced and sold needs to be counted; it makes sense only to include final goods and services. A farmer sells wheat to a flour mill for Rs 20 per kg. The mill sells flour to a biscuit company for Rs 25 per kg. The company makes four packets of biscuits and sells them for Rs 80 (Rs 20 per packet). Biscuits are final goods, goods that reach the consumers. Wheat and flour are intermediate goods, used up in producing final goods. The value of final goods already includes the value of all intermediate goods. The value of Rs 80 for biscuits already includes the value of flour (Rs 25). Counting flour and wheat separately would count the same things a number of times.

question_english: If 10,000 kg of wheat is sold at ₹20 per kg and 5,000 coconuts at ₹15 each, what is the total value of these goods?
question_hinglish: Agar 10,000 kg gehun ₹20 per kg aur 5,000 nariyal ₹15 per nariyal bikte hain, toh in cheezon ki kul keemat kya hai?
answer_english: Value of wheat = 10,000 × 20 = ₹2,00,000. Value of coconuts = 5,000 × 15 = ₹75,000. Total value = 2,00,000 + 75,000 = ₹2,75,000. Economists add values rather than quantities because quantities of different goods cannot be added.

subject: Social Science
question_english: A farmer sells wheat to a mill for ₹20, the mill sells flour for ₹25, and a biscuit company sells biscuits for ₹80. Using the value-added method, how much value is added at each stage, and what is the total?
question_hinglish: Ek kisan mill ko ₹20 ka gehun bechta hai, mill ₹25 ka aata bechti hai, aur biscuit company ₹80 ke biscuits bechti hai. Value-added method se har charan mein kitni keemat judi, aur kul kitni?
answer_english: Farmer adds ₹20 (assuming no inputs). Mill adds 25 − 20 = ₹5. Biscuit company adds 80 − 25 = ₹55 (it also uses sugar and oil, but here we take the difference). Total value added = 20 + 5 + 55 = ₹80, which equals the value of the final good, so counting only the final good avoids double counting.
answer_hinglish: Kisan ne ₹20 jode (maante hue koi input nahi). Mill ne 25 − 20 = ₹5 jode. Biscuit company ne 80 − 25 = ₹55 jode (woh cheeni aur tel bhi lagaati hai, par yahan antar le rahe hain). Kul judi keemat = 20 + 5 + 55 = ₹80, jo final good ki keemat ke barabar hai, isliye sirf final good ginne se dohri ginti nahi hoti.

question_english: What does the history of developed countries indicate about shifts between sectors?
question_hinglish: Viksit deshon ka itihaas sectors ke beech badlav ke baare mein kya batata hai?
answer_english: At initial stages of development, the primary sector was the most important; as farming improved and produced more food, people took up crafts and trade. Over a hundred years, with new manufacturing methods, factories expanded and people moved from farms to factories, so the secondary sector became most important in production and employment. In the past 100 years, there has been a further shift to the tertiary sector, which now dominates production and employs most working people in developed countries.
answer_hinglish: Vikaas ki shuruaat mein primary sector sabse important tha; kheti sudhrane aur zyada anaaj paida hone pe log shilp aur vyapaar karne lage. Sau saal mein naye manufacturing tareekon se factories faili aur log kheton se factories mein gaye, isliye secondary sector utpaadan aur rozgaar mein sabse important bana. Pichhle 100 saal mein tertiary sector ki taraf aur badlav hua, jo ab viksit deshon mein utpaadan pe haavi hai aur zyadatar logon ko rozgaar deta hai.
ncert_context: From the histories of many developed countries, at initial stages of development, the primary sector was the most important. The secondary sector gradually became the most important in total production and employment. The service sector has become the most important in total production, and most working people are employed in it.

question_english: Why is the tertiary sector becoming so important in India?
question_hinglish: India mein tertiary sector itna important kyun ho raha hai?
answer_english: First, basic services like hospitals, schools, post and telegraph, police, courts, municipal bodies, defence, transport, banks and insurance are needed, and in a developing country the government must provide them. Fourth, new services based on information and communication technology have become essential and are growing rapidly.

question_english: Why has a shift out of the primary sector not happened in employment in India, as it has in production?

subject: Social Science
question_english: What do you understand by disguised unemployment? Explain with rural and urban examples.
question_hinglish: Disguised unemployment se tum kya samajhte ho? Grameen aur shehri examples se samjhao.
answer_english: Disguised unemployment, or underemployment, is when people appear to be working but all are working less than their potential, and their labour effort is divided; it is hidden, unlike open unemployment. Rural example: all five members of small farmer Laxmi's family work on her two-hectare unirrigated plot, but two could leave without production falling. Urban example: casual workers like painters, plumbers and repair persons who search for daily work and don't find it every day, or street vendors who spend the whole day but earn very little.
answer_hinglish: Disguised unemployment, yaani underemployment, tab hoti hai jab log kaam karte dikhte hain par sab apni kshamta se kam kaam karte hain aur unki mehnat bat jaati hai; yeh khuli berozgaari ke ulat chhupi hoti hai. Grameen example: chhoti kisan Laxmi ke parivaar ke paancho log uski do hectare bina sinchaai ki zameen pe kaam karte hain, par do log bina utpaadan ghataye ja sakte hain. Shehri example: painters, plumbers aur marammat karne wale jaise dihaadi mazdoor jo roz kaam dhundhte hain par roz nahi milta, ya pheriwale jo din bhar kaam karke bhi bahut kam kamaate hain.
ncert_context: There are more people in agriculture than necessary; even if you move a few out, production will not be affected. Workers in agriculture are underemployed. Laxmi, a small farmer owning about two hectares of unirrigated land growing jowar and arhar, has all five family members working on the plot throughout the year because they have nowhere else to go. Everyone is working but no one is fully employed. This is underemployment, where people are apparently working but all are made to work less than their potential. This underemployment is hidden in contrast to someone without a job who is clearly visible as unemployed; hence it is called disguised unemployment. Underemployment also happens in services: thousands of casual workers in urban areas search for daily employment as painters, plumbers, repair persons doing odd jobs; many don't find work every day. People on the street pushing a cart or selling something may spend the whole day but earn very little.

subject: Social Science
question_english: What is MGNREGA 2005, and why is it called 'Right to Work'?
question_hinglish: MGNREGA 2005 kya hai, aur ise 'Right to Work' kyun kehte hain?
answer_english: Recognising the need for quick short-term measures, the government made a law implementing the Right to Work in about 625 districts, called the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA). It guaranteed 100 days of employment a year to all who are able to and need work in rural areas; if the government failed, it would pay unemployment allowances. Work that would increase production from land was preferred. It is called 'Right to Work' because it legally guarantees employment. In 2025 it was replaced by the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Viksit Bharat-G RAM G 2025).
answer_hinglish: Jaldi asar wale kadamon ki zaroorat samajh kar sarkar ne lagbhag 625 districts mein Right to Work laagu karne wala kanoon banaya, Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA). Isne gaon mein kaam karne layak aur zarooratmand sabko saal mein 100 din rozgaar ki guarantee di; sarkar na de paaye toh berozgaari bhatta deti. Zameen se utpaadan badhane wale kaam ko tarjeeh di gayi. Ise 'Right to Work' isliye kehte hain kyunki yeh kanooni roop se rozgaar guarantee karta hai. 2025 mein ise Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Viksit Bharat-G RAM G 2025) ne badla.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Compare the employment conditions in the organised and unorganised sectors.
question_hinglish: Organised aur unorganised sectors mein rozgaar ki sthitiyon ki tulna karo.
answer_english: The organised sector covers enterprises with regular terms of employment, registered by the government and following laws like the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and Shops and Establishments Act. Workers have job security, fixed hours with overtime pay, paid leave, holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits, safe working conditions and pensions. The unorganised sector has small, scattered units largely outside government control; rules exist but are not followed, jobs are low-paid, irregular and insecure, with no overtime, paid leave or sick leave, and workers can be asked to leave anytime.
answer_hinglish: Organised sector mein niyamit rozgaar wale udyam hain, jo sarkar mein registered hain aur Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act aur Shops and Establishments Act jaise kanoon maante hain. Mazdooron ko naukri ki suraksha, fixed ghante aur overtime, chhutti, holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical fayde, surakshit maahaul aur pension milti hai. Unorganised sector mein chhoti, bikhri ikaiyan hain jo zyadatar sarkari niyantran se bahar hain; niyam hain par maane nahi jaate, naukriyan kam paise wali, aniyamit aur asurakshit hain, overtime, chhutti ya beemaari ki chhutti nahi, aur kabhi bhi nikaala ja sakta hai.

Workers enjoy security of employment, work fixed hours, get overtime, paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits, safe working environment and pensions. The unorganised sector is characterised by small and scattered units largely outside the control of government. There are rules and regulations but these are not followed. Jobs are low-paid and often not regular. There is no provision for overtime, paid leave, holidays or sick leave. Employment is not secure; people can be asked to leave without any reason.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Why do workers in the unorganised sector need protection, and who are they?
question_hinglish: Unorganised sector ke mazdooron ko suraksha kyun chahiye, aur woh kaun hain?
answer_english: Organised sector jobs expand slowly, some organised enterprises operate in the unorganised sector to evade taxes and labour laws, and since the 1990s many organised workers lost jobs, pushing more people into low-paid, irregular, insecure unorganised work where they are exploited and denied fair wages. In rural areas, they are landless labourers, small and marginal farmers (nearly 80 per cent of rural households), sharecroppers and artisans; in urban areas, small-scale industry workers, casual construction, trade and transport workers, street vendors, head-load workers, garment makers and rag pickers. Many are SCs, STs and backward communities who also face social discrimination.
answer_hinglish: Organised sector ki naukriyan dheere badhti hain, kuch organised udyam tax aur shram kanoonon se bachne ke liye unorganised sector mein chalte hain, aur 1990s se kai organised mazdooron ki naukri gayi, jisse zyada log kam paise wali, aniyamit aur asurakshit unorganised naukriyon mein dhakele gaye jahan unka shoshan hota hai. Gaon mein yeh bhoomiheen mazdoor, chhote aur seemaant kisan (lagbhag 80 percent grameen ghar), bataidaar aur kaarigar hain; shehron mein chhote udyog ke mazdoor, nirmaan, vyapaar aur transport ke dihaadi mazdoor, pheriwale, headload mazdoor, darzi aur kachra beenne wale. Kai SCs, STs aur pichhde samudaayon se hain jo samajik bhed-bhaav bhi jhelte hain.
ncert_context: Employment opportunities in the organised sector have been expanding very slowly. Many organised sector enterprises are found in the unorganised sector to evade taxes and refuse to follow labour laws. Workers are forced into unorganised sector jobs which pay very low salary, are often exploited and not paid a fair wage. Since the 1990s, many workers lost jobs in the organised sector. Nearly 80 per cent of rural households are small and marginal farmers. In urban areas, it comprises workers in small-scale industry, casual workers in construction, trade and transport, street vendors, head load workers, garment makers, rag pickers. A majority of workers from scheduled castes, tribes and backward communities are in the unorganised sector and also face social discrimination.

question_english: Distinguish between the public and private sectors.
question_hinglish: Public aur private sector mein fark batao.
answer_english: Sectors are classified on the basis of ownership of assets and responsibility for delivering services. subject: Social Science
question_english: Why does the government take up activities in the public sector? Give examples.
question_hinglish: Sarkar public sector mein gatividhiyan kyun karti hai? Examples do.
answer_english: Some things society needs, like roads, bridges, railways, harbours, electricity and irrigation dams, need huge spending beyond the private sector's capacity, and collecting charges from users is hard, so private firms would charge high rates; the government ensures they are available to all. The government also supports activities, like supplying electricity at affordable rates to small industries or buying wheat and rice at fair prices from farmers and selling cheaper through ration shops, supporting both farmers and consumers. It is also responsible for health, education, safe drinking water, housing, nutrition and developing backward regions.
answer_hinglish: Samaaj ko sadkein, pul, railways, bandargaah, bijli aur sinchaai dams jaisi cheezein chahiye jinme private sector ki kshamta se zyada kharch lagta hai aur upyog karne walon se paisa ikattha karna mushkil hai, isliye private companies zyada daam lengi; sarkar inhe sabke liye uplabdh banati hai. Sarkar chhote udyogon ko sasti bijli dena ya kisaanon se uchit daam pe gehun aur chawal khareed kar ration dukaanon pe saste mein bechna jaise kaam bhi karti hai, jisse kisaan aur upbhokta dono ko sahara milta hai. Sehat, shiksha, saaf paani, ghar, poshan aur pichhde ilaakon ka vikaas bhi uski zimmedari hai.
ncert_context: There are things needed by society that the private sector will not provide at reasonable cost because they need large sums of money and collecting money from thousands of users is not easy; examples are roads, bridges, railways, harbours, generating electricity, irrigation through dams. Governments undertake such spending to ensure facilities are available to everyone. Selling electricity at cost of generation may push up production costs and shut down small units; government supplies electricity at affordable rates, bearing part of the cost. The Government buys wheat and rice from farmers at a 'fair price', stores them and sells at a lower price through ration shops, supporting both farmers and consumers. Providing health and education facilities for all is the government's responsibility, as is attention to safe drinking water, housing for the poor, food and nutrition, and the poorest and most ignored regions.

subject: Social Science
question_english: 'The tertiary sector is not playing any significant role in the development of the Indian economy.' Do you agree?
question_hinglish: 'Tertiary sector Indian economy ke vikaas mein koi khaas bhoomika nahi nibha raha.' Kya tum sahmat ho?
answer_english: No. The tertiary sector became the largest producing sector by 2017-18, contributing over half of GVA, and it supports the primary and secondary sectors through transport, storage, communication, banking and trade. It provides basic services like health, education and administration, meets rising demand for services as incomes grow, and includes fast-growing IT services. However, only part of it employs skilled workers well; many in it earn little, so its benefits are uneven.
answer_hinglish: Nahi. 2017-18 tak tertiary sector sabse bada utpaadak sector ban gaya aur GVA ka aadhe se zyada deta hai, aur transport, bhandaaran, sanchaar, banking aur vyapaar se primary aur secondary sectors ko sahara deta hai. Yeh sehat, shiksha aur prashaasan jaisi mool sevayein deta hai, aamdani badhne pe badhti sevaon ki demand poori karta hai, aur isme tezi se badhti IT sevayein hain. Par iska sirf ek hissa kushal logon ko achha rozgaar deta hai; kai log bahut kam kamaate hain, isliye fayde asamaan hain.
ncert_context: Over the forty years between 1977–78 and 2017–18, production increased the most in the tertiary sector, which emerged as the largest producing sector in India. Tertiary activities help the development of primary and secondary sectors: transport, storage, communication, banking, trade. Basic services such as hospitals, education, police, courts, banks are required. As income levels rise, people demand more services. New services based on information and communication technology have become essential. However, not all of the service sector is growing equally; many workers like small shopkeepers and repair persons barely earn a living.

question_english: Fill in the blanks: Cotton is a ______ product and cloth is a ______ product, and activities in the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors are ______.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Is the classification of economic activities into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors useful?
question_hinglish: Kya economic gatividhiyon ko primary, secondary aur tertiary sectors mein baantna upyogi hai?
answer_english: Yes. Classification helps us think usefully and analyse a situation. Using the criterion of 'nature of activity', the three-sector classification lets us analyse the pattern of total production and employment, for example showing that in India the tertiary sector is the largest producer while the primary sector remains the largest employer, which reveals underemployment and the need to create jobs in other sectors.
answer_hinglish: Haan. Bantwara upyogi tareeke se sochne aur sthiti ko samajhne mein madad karta hai. 'Gatividhi ke swabhaav' ke aadhaar pe teen sector wala bantwara kul utpaadan aur rozgaar ka pattern samajhne deta hai, jaise yeh dikhana ki India mein tertiary sector sabse bada utpaadak hai jabki primary sector sabse bada rozgaar deta hai, jisse underemployment aur doosre sectors mein naukriyan banane ki zaroorat saamne aati hai.
ncert_context: With so many activities taking place, one needs the process of classification to think in a useful manner. The criterion could be many depending on what we desire to find out. Classification helps to analyse a situation. In dividing economic activities into three sectors, the criterion used was the 'nature of activity'. On the basis of this classification, we were able to analyse the pattern of total production and employment in India. While goods and services produced in the tertiary sector contribute the most, employment remains in the primary sector.

subject: Social Science
question_english: What is meant by double coincidence of wants?
question_hinglish: Double coincidence of wants ka kya matlab hai?
answer_english: Double coincidence of wants is when both parties agree to sell and buy each other's commodities, so what one person desires to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy. For example, a shoe manufacturer wanting wheat must find a farmer who sells wheat and also wants to buy shoes. It is an essential feature of the barter system.
answer_hinglish: Double coincidence of wants tab hota hai jab dono log ek-doosre ka saamaan bechne aur khareedne ko raazi hon, yaani jo ek bechna chahta hai wahi doosra khareedna chahta hai. Jaise gehun chaahne wale joote banane wale ko aisa kisan dhundhna padega jo gehun bechta ho aur joote bhi khareedna chahta ho. Yeh barter system ki zaroori pehchaan hai.
ncert_context: Take the case of a shoe manufacturer who wants to sell shoes and buy wheat. Without money, he would have to look for a wheat growing farmer who not only wants to sell wheat but also wants to buy the shoes in exchange. That is, both parties have to agree to sell and buy each others commodities. This is known as double coincidence of wants. What a person desires to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy. In a barter system where goods are directly exchanged without the use of money, double coincidence of wants is an essential feature.

subject: Social Science
question_english: How does money solve the problem of double coincidence of wants?
question_hinglish: Paisa double coincidence of wants ki samasya kaise suljhata hai?
answer_english: Money acts as the crucial intermediate step in exchange. The shoe manufacturer first exchanges shoes for money and then uses the money to buy wheat or any other commodity. He only needs to find a buyer for his shoes, not a farmer who both sells wheat and wants shoes. Since everyone accepts money, it eliminates the need for double coincidence of wants and is called a medium of exchange.
answer_hinglish: Paisa len-den mein beech ki zaroori kadi ka kaam karta hai. Joote banane wala pehle joote paise ke badle bechta hai, phir us paise se gehun ya koi bhi cheez khareedta hai. Use sirf joote ka khareedaar dhundhna hai, aisa kisan nahi jo gehun bhi bechta ho aur joote bhi chahta ho. Kyunki sab paisa lete hain, yeh double coincidence of wants ki zaroorat khatam karta hai aur ise medium of exchange kehte hain.
ncert_context: A person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service that he or she might want. Thus everyone prefers to receive payments in money and then exchange the money for things that they want. The shoe manufacturer will first exchange shoes that he has produced for money, and then exchange the money for wheat. In an economy where money is in use, money by providing the crucial intermediate step eliminates the need for double coincidence of wants. It is no longer necessary for the shoe manufacturer to look for a farmer who will buy his shoes and at the same time sell him wheat. All he has to do is find a buyer for his shoes. Since money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, it is called a medium of exchange.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Why is modern currency accepted as a medium of exchange even though it has no use of its own?
question_hinglish: Modern currency ka khud ka koi upyog nahi hai, phir bhi ise medium of exchange kyun maana jaata hai?
answer_english: Modern currency of paper notes and coins is not made of precious metals and has no use of its own, unlike grain or cattle. It is accepted because it is authorised by the government of the country. In India, the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government, no other individual or organisation may issue currency, and the law legalises the rupee as a payment that cannot be refused in India.
answer_hinglish: Kaagaz ke note aur sikke wali modern currency keemti dhaatu ki nahi bani aur anaaj ya pashuon ki tarah iska khud ka koi upyog nahi. Ise isliye maana jaata hai kyunki desh ki sarkar ne ise authorise kiya hai. India mein Reserve Bank of India central government ki taraf se note jaari karta hai, koi aur vyakti ya sanstha currency jaari nahi kar sakti, aur kanoon rupee ko aisa bhugtaan banata hai jise India mein mana nahi kiya ja sakta.

question_english: What are demand deposits?
question_hinglish: Demand deposits kya hote hain?
answer_english: Demand deposits are deposits people keep in bank accounts that can be withdrawn on demand. People deposit extra cash with banks, where it is safe and earns interest, and they can withdraw it whenever they need it.
answer_hinglish: Demand deposits woh jama paise hain jo log bank accounts mein rakhte hain aur maangne pe nikaal sakte hain. Log apna faltu cash bank mein jama karte hain, jahan woh surakshit rehta hai aur interest kamaata hai, aur zaroorat pe kabhi bhi nikaala ja sakta hai.
ncert_context: The other form in which people hold money is as deposits with banks. At a point of time, people need only some currency for their day-to-day needs. Workers who receive salaries at the end of each month have extra cash at the beginning of the month. They deposit it with the banks by opening a bank account in their name. Banks accept the deposits and also pay an amount as interest on the deposits. In this way people's money is safe with the banks and it earns interest. People also have the provision to withdraw the money as and when they require. Since the deposits in the bank accounts can be withdrawn on demand, these deposits are called demand deposits.

question_english: Why are demand deposits considered as money?
question_hinglish: Demand deposits ko paisa kyun maana jaata hai?
answer_english: Demand deposits share the essential feature of money, being a medium of exchange. Through the cheque facility, payments can be settled directly from one bank account to another without using cash. Since demand deposits are accepted widely as a means of payment, along with currency, they constitute money in the modern economy.
answer_hinglish: Demand deposits mein paise ki zaroori khoobi hai, yaani medium of exchange hona. Cheque ki suvidha se bina cash ke ek bank account se doosre mein bhugtaan ho jaata hai. ncert_context: Demand deposits offer another interesting facility. It is this facility which lends it the essential characteristics of money (that of a medium of exchange). The facility of cheques against demand deposits makes it possible to directly settle payments without the use of cash. Since demand deposits are accepted widely as a means of payment, along with currency, they constitute money in the modern economy.

question_english: What was demonetisation in India, and how did it promote digital transactions?
question_hinglish: India mein demonetisation kya tha, aur isne digital transactions ko kaise badhaava diya?
answer_english: In November 2016, currency notes of ₹500 and ₹1,000 were declared invalid; people had to surrender them to banks within a specific period and receive new ₹500, ₹2,000 or other notes. Since then people were encouraged to use bank deposits rather than cash, so digital transactions spread through internet or mobile bank transfers, cheques, ATM cards, credit cards, POS swipe machines and QR codes through UPI. This was promoted to reduce the need for cash and control corruption.
answer_hinglish: November 2016 mein ₹500 aur ₹1,000 ke note avaidh ghoshit kiye gaye; logon ko tay samay mein inhe bank mein jama karke naye ₹500, ₹2,000 ya doosre note lene the. Tab se logon ko cash ki jagah bank deposits use karne ko kaha gaya, isliye internet ya mobile se bank transfer, cheques, ATM cards, credit cards, POS swipe machines aur UPI ke QR codes se digital transactions faile. Iska maqsad cash ki zaroorat ghatana aur corruption rokna tha.

subject: Social Science
question_english: How do banks mediate between those who have surplus money and those who need money?
question_hinglish: Banks faltu paise wale logon aur paise ki zaroorat wale logon ke beech madhyasth kaise bante hain?
answer_english: Banks accept deposits from people with surplus funds and pay them interest. They keep only a small proportion, about 5 per cent in India, as cash to pay depositors who withdraw on any given day, and use the major portion to give loans to borrowers. Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits, and this difference is their main source of income.
answer_hinglish: Banks faltu paise wale logon se deposits lete hain aur unhe interest dete hain. Woh sirf chhota hissa, India mein lagbhag 5 percent, cash mein rakhte hain taaki kisi din paise nikaalne wale depositors ko de sakein, aur zyada hissa borrowers ko loan dene mein lagaate hain. Banks loans pe deposits se zyada interest lete hain, aur yahi antar unki aamdani ka mukhya zariya hai.
ncert_context: Banks keep only a small proportion of their deposits as cash with themselves. For example, banks in India these days hold about 5 per cent of their deposits as cash. This is kept as provision to pay the depositors who might come to withdraw money from the bank on any given day. Since, on any particular day, only some of its many depositors come to withdraw cash, the bank is able to manage with this cash. Banks use the major portion of the deposits to extend loans. Banks make use of the deposits to meet the loan requirements of the people. In this way, banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (the depositors) and those who are in need of these funds (the borrowers). Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than what they offer on deposits. The difference between what is charged from borrowers and what is paid to depositors is their main source of income.

question_english: What is a debt trap?
question_hinglish: Debt trap kya hai?
answer_english: A debt trap is a situation where credit, instead of improving the borrower's earnings, pushes them into a position from which recovery is very painful. For example, Swapna's crop failed, she could not repay her loan, and she had to sell part of her land.
answer_hinglish: Debt trap aisi sthiti hai jahan credit lene wale ki aamdani badhane ki jagah use aisi haalat mein dhakel deta hai jisse ubharna bahut dardnaak hota hai. Jaise Swapna ki fasal kharaab hui, woh karz nahi chuka paayi, aur use zameen ka hissa bechna pada.

Credit in this case pushes the borrower into a situation from which recovery is very painful.

subject: Social Science
question_english: In situations with high risks, credit might create further problems for the borrower. Explain.
question_hinglish: Zyada jokhim wali sthitiyon mein credit lene wale ke liye aur samasyayein paida kar sakta hai. Samjhao.
answer_english: In rural areas, crop loans are taken at the start of the season and repaid after harvest, so repayment depends on farm income. If the crop fails due to pests or climate, the borrower cannot repay, and the debt grows. As with Swapna, a fresh loan taken next year may not cover the old one, and the borrower may have to sell assets like land. So whether credit helps depends on the risks and whether there is support in case of loss.
answer_hinglish: Gaon mein fasal ke loan season ki shuruaat mein liye jaate hain aur kataai ke baad chukaaye jaate hain, isliye chukaana kheti ki aamdani pe nirbhar hai. Agar keedon ya mausam se fasal kharaab ho jaaye, toh karz nahi chukta aur badhta jaata hai. Swapna ki tarah agle saal liya naya loan purana karz nahi chuka paata, aur zameen jaisi sampatti bechni pad sakti hai. Isliye credit faydemand hai ya nahi, yeh jokhim aur nuksaan ke samay sahaare pe nirbhar hai.
ncert_context: In rural areas, the main demand for credit is for crop production. Crop production involves considerable costs on seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, water, electricity, repair of equipment. There is a minimum stretch of three to four months between buying inputs and selling the crop. Farmers usually take crop loans at the beginning of the season and repay the loan after harvest. Repayment is crucially dependent on income from farming. In Swapna's case, the failure of the crop made loan repayment impossible. She had to sell part of the land. Credit left her worse off. Whether credit would be useful or not, therefore, depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is some support, in case of loss.

subject: Social Science
question_english: What is collateral? Give examples.
question_hinglish: Collateral kya hai? Examples do.
answer_english: Collateral is an asset that the borrower owns and uses as a guarantee to a lender until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay, the lender has the right to sell the collateral to obtain payment. Examples include land titles, buildings, vehicles, livestock and deposits with banks.
answer_hinglish: Collateral lene wale ki apni sampatti hai jise woh loan chukne tak dene wale ke paas guarantee ke roop mein rakhta hai. ncert_context: Every loan agreement specifies an interest rate which the borrower must pay to the lender along with the repayment of the principal. In addition, lenders may demand collateral (security) against loans. Collateral is an asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle, livestocks, deposits with banks) and uses this as a guarantee to a lender until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay the loan, the lender has the right to sell the asset or collateral to obtain payment. Property such as land titles, deposits with banks, livestock are some common examples of collateral used for borrowing.

If the borrower fails to repay the loan, the lender has the right to sell the asset or collateral to obtain payment. Property such as land titles, deposits with banks, livestock are some common examples of collateral used for borrowing.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Shyamal, a small farmer in Sonpur with 1.5 acres, borrows from an agricultural trader. What are the terms of his credit?
question_hinglish: Sonpur ka chhota kisan Shyamal, jiske paas 1.5 acre zameen hai, ek agricultural trader se udhaar leta hai. Uske credit ki shartein kya hain?
answer_english: Earlier Shyamal borrowed from the village moneylender at 5 per cent per month (60 per cent per annum). Now he borrows from a trader at 3 per cent per month; the trader supplies farm inputs on credit at the start of the season, to be repaid at harvest. The trader also makes farmers promise to sell their crop to him, ensuring prompt repayment and buying the crop at low post-harvest prices to sell later at higher prices.
answer_hinglish: Pehle Shyamal gaon ke moneylender se 5 percent per mahina (60 percent saalana) pe udhaar leta tha. Ab woh trader se 3 percent per mahina pe leta hai; trader season ki shuruaat mein kheti ka saamaan udhaar deta hai, jo kataai pe chukaana hota hai. Trader kisaanon se fasal use hi bechne ka vaada bhi leta hai, jisse paisa jaldi waapas aata hai aur woh kataai ke baad saste mein fasal khareed kar baad mein mehenge daam pe bechta hai.
ncert_context: Shyamal tells us that every season he needs loans for cultivation on his 1.5 acres of land. At the beginning of the cropping season, the trader supplies the farm inputs on credit, which is to be repaid when the crops are ready for harvest. Besides the interest charge on the loan, the trader also makes the farmers promise to sell the crop to him. This way the trader can ensure that the money is repaid promptly. Also, since the crop prices are low after the harvest, the trader is able to make a profit from buying the crop at a low price from the farmers and then selling it later when the price has risen.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Describe Rama's credit situation in Sonpur. Why will her debt keep rising?
question_hinglish: Sonpur mein Rama ki credit sthiti batao. Uska karz badhta kyun rahega?
answer_english: Rama is a landless agricultural labourer with no work for several months a year, so she borrows for daily expenses, illnesses and family functions. Her only source is her employer, a medium landowner, who charges 5 per cent per month; she repays by working for him. She usually takes a fresh loan before the previous one is repaid and owes ₹5,000. Though he treats her badly, she depends on him, so her debt keeps rising.
answer_hinglish: Rama bhoomiheen khet mazdoor hai jiske paas saal ke kai mahine kaam nahi hota, isliye woh roz ke kharch, beemaari aur parivaar ke function ke liye udhaar leti hai. subject: Social Science
question_english: How do cooperative societies provide cheap credit in rural areas? Explain with the example of Krishak Cooperative.
question_hinglish: Cooperative societies gaon mein sasta credit kaise deti hain? Krishak Cooperative ke example se samjhao.
answer_english: Besides banks, cooperatives are a major source of cheap rural credit; members pool their resources for cooperation. Krishak Cooperative has 2300 farmer members and accepts deposits from them. Using these deposits as collateral, it obtains a large bank loan and lends to members; once repaid, another round of lending can take place. It gives loans for agricultural implements, cultivation, agricultural trade, fisheries, house construction and other expenses.
answer_hinglish: Banks ke alaava cooperatives gaon mein saste credit ka bada zariya hain; sadasya apne sansaadhan milaate hain. In deposits ko collateral banakar woh bank se bada loan leti hai aur sadasyon ko udhaar deti hai; chukne pe phir se udhaar diya ja sakta hai. Yeh kheti ke auzaar, kheti, krishi vyapaar, machhli palan, ghar banane aur doosre kharchon ke liye loan deti hai.
ncert_context: Besides banks, the other major source of cheap credit in rural areas are the cooperative societies (or cooperatives). Members of a cooperative pool their resources for cooperation in certain areas. There are several types of cooperatives possible such as farmers cooperatives, weavers cooperatives, industrial workers cooperatives, etc. Krishak Cooperative functions in a village not very far away from Sonpur. It has 2300 farmers as members. It accepts deposits from its members. With these deposits as collateral, the Cooperative has obtained a large loan from the bank. These funds are used to provide loans to members. Once these loans are repaid, another round of lending can take place. Krishak Cooperative provides loans for the purchase of agricultural implements, loans for cultivation and agricultural trade, fishery loans, loans for construction of houses and for a variety of other expenses.

subject: Social Science
question_english: What are the differences between formal and informal sources of credit?
question_hinglish: Credit ke formal aur informal sources mein kya fark hai?
answer_english: Formal sources include banks and cooperatives; they are supervised by the RBI, charge lower interest, and require collateral and documents. Informal sources include moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends; no organisation supervises them, so they can charge whatever interest they choose, usually much higher, and may use unfair means to recover money. Informal lenders know borrowers personally and often lend without collateral.
answer_hinglish: Formal sources mein banks aur cooperatives hain; RBI inki nigraani karta hai, yeh kam interest lete hain, aur collateral aur documents maangte hain. Informal sources mein moneylenders, traders, maalik, rishtedaar aur dost hain; inki koi nigraani nahi, isliye yeh manchaaha, aksar bahut zyada interest le sakte hain aur paisa vasoolne ke liye galat tareeke apna sakte hain. Informal lenders lene walon ko nijee roop se jaante hain aur aksar bina collateral udhaar dete hain.
ncert_context: The various types of loans can be grouped as formal sector loans and informal sector loans. Among the former are loans from banks and cooperatives. The informal lenders include moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends, etc. The Reserve Bank of India supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans. There is no organisation which supervises the credit activities of lenders in the informal sector. They can lend at whatever interest rate they choose. There is no one to stop them from using unfair means to get their money back. Compared to the formal lenders, most of the informal lenders charge a much higher interest on loans. Bank loans require proper documents and collateral. Moneylenders know the borrowers personally and are often willing to give a loan without collateral.

subject: Social Science
question_english: In what ways does the Reserve Bank of India supervise the functioning of banks? Why is this necessary?
question_hinglish: Reserve Bank of India banks ke kaam ki nigraani kin tareekon se karta hai? Yeh zaroori kyun hai?
answer_english: The RBI monitors whether banks actually maintain a minimum cash balance out of their deposits. It ensures banks lend not just to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers. Banks must periodically report to the RBI how much they lend, to whom and at what interest rate. This is necessary to keep depositors' money safe and to make sure cheap credit reaches those who need it.
answer_hinglish: RBI dekhta hai ki banks apne deposits mein se zaroori minimum cash balance sach mein rakhte hain ya nahi. Woh yeh bhi pakka karta hai ki banks sirf munaafe wale business aur traders ko nahi, balki chhote kisaanon, chhote udyogon aur chhote borrowers ko bhi loan dein. Banks ko samay-samay pe RBI ko batana padta hai ki woh kitna, kise aur kis interest rate pe loan de rahe hain. Yeh depositors ka paisa surakshit rakhne aur zarooratmandon tak sasta credit pahunchaane ke liye zaroori hai.

question_english: Why is the high cost of informal credit harmful to borrowers?
question_hinglish: Informal credit ki zyada keemat borrowers ke liye nuksaandeh kyun hai?
answer_english: Higher interest means a larger part of the borrower's earnings goes to repaying the loan, leaving less income for themselves, as with Shyamal. question_english: Why is the share of formal sector credit higher for richer households than poorer households? What does this suggest?
question_hinglish: Ameer gharon ke liye formal credit ka hissa gareeb gharon se zyada kyun hai? Isse kya pata chalta hai?
answer_english: In urban areas, 54 per cent of loans of poor households come from informal sources, while for rich households only 17 per cent are informal and 83 per cent formal; rural areas show a similar pattern. Banks require collateral and documents, which the rich can provide and the poor often cannot, so the poor depend on costly informal lenders. This suggests formal credit must expand and be distributed more equally so the poor benefit from cheaper loans.
answer_hinglish: Shehron mein gareeb gharon ke 54 percent loans informal sources se aate hain, jabki ameer gharon ke sirf 17 percent informal aur 83 percent formal hain; gaon mein bhi aisa hi pattern hai. Banks collateral aur documents maangte hain jo ameer de sakte hain par gareeb aksar nahi, isliye gareeb mehenge informal lenders pe nirbhar hain. Isse pata chalta hai ki formal credit badhna aur zyada barabari se baantna chahiye taaki gareebon ko sasta loan mile.
ncert_context: Graph 2 shows the importance of formal and informal sources of credit for people in urban areas, divided into four groups from poor to rich. 54 per cent of the loans taken by poor households in the urban areas are from informal sources. The rich households are availing cheap credit from formal lenders whereas the poor households have to pay a large amount for borrowing. Absence of collateral is one of the major reasons which prevents the poor from getting bank loans. It is important that formal credit is distributed more equally so that the poor can benefit from the cheaper loans.

answer_english: Manav will compare the terms of credit: interest rate, collateral, documentation and repayment conditions. A bank charges much lower interest and is supervised by the RBI, but needs collateral and proper documents. A moneylender may lend without collateral and knows him personally, but charges very high interest, keeps no records and may harass borrowers. If he can provide collateral and documents, the bank loan is better, since high interest would eat into his business earnings.
answer_hinglish: Manav terms of credit ki tulna karega: interest rate, collateral, documents aur chukaane ki shartein. Bank bahut kam interest leta hai aur RBI ki nigraani mein hai, par collateral aur sahi documents maangta hai. Moneylender bina collateral de sakta hai aur use jaanta hai, par bahut zyada interest leta hai, record nahi rakhta aur pareshaan kar sakta hai. Agar woh collateral aur documents de sake, toh bank loan behtar hai, kyunki zyada interest business ki kamaai kha jaayega.
ncert_context: Interest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment together comprise the terms of credit. Bank loans require proper documents and collateral. Informal lenders such as moneylenders know the borrowers personally and are often willing to give a loan without collateral. However, the moneylenders charge very high rates of interest, keep no records of the transactions and harass the poor borrowers. The RBI supervises formal lenders. Higher cost of borrowing means a larger part of the earnings of the borrowers is used to repay the loan.

subject: Social Science
question_english: What is the basic idea behind Self Help Groups (SHGs) for the poor?
question_hinglish: Gareebon ke liye Self Help Groups (SHGs) ka mool vichaar kya hai?
answer_english: The idea is to organise the rural poor, especially women, into small groups of 15-20 members from one neighbourhood who meet and save regularly, ₹25 to ₹100 or more each. Members take small loans from the group at less interest than moneylenders charge. After a year or two of regular saving, the group can get a bank loan in its name for self-employment. Since the group is responsible for repayment, banks lend without collateral.
answer_hinglish: Vichaar hai gaon ke gareebon, khaas kar mahilaon, ko ek mohalle ke 15-20 sadasyon ke chhote groups mein sangathit karna jo milte hain aur niyamit bachat karte hain, har koi ₹25 se ₹100 ya zyada. Sadasya group se moneylender se kam interest pe chhote loan lete hain. Ek-do saal niyamit bachat ke baad group apne naam pe swarozgaar ke liye bank loan le sakta hai. Kyunki chukaane ki zimmedari group ki hai, banks bina collateral udhaar dete hain.
ncert_context: The idea is to organise rural poor, in particular women, into small Self Help Groups (SHGs) and pool (collect) their savings. A typical SHG has 15-20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly. Saving per member varies from Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more, depending on the ability of the people to save. Members can take small loans from the group itself to meet their needs. The group charges interest on these loans but this is still less than what the moneylender charges. After a year or two, if the group is regular in savings, it becomes eligible for availing loan from the bank. Loan is sanctioned in the name of the group and is meant to create self-employment opportunities for the members. It is the group which is responsible for the repayment of the loan. Because of this feature, banks are willing to lend to the poor women when organised in SHGs, even though they have no collateral as such.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Why are banks willing to lend to poor women organised in SHGs even without collateral, and what other benefits do SHGs offer?
question_hinglish: Banks SHGs mein sangathit gareeb mahilaon ko bina collateral bhi udhaar kyun dete hain, aur SHGs ke aur kya fayde hain?
answer_english: The group, not an individual, is responsible for repaying the loan, and any non-repayment by one member is followed up seriously by other members, so banks lend even without collateral. SHGs thus overcome the lack of collateral and provide timely loans at reasonable interest. They are building blocks of organisation of the rural poor, help women become financially self-reliant, and their regular meetings provide a platform to discuss social issues like health, nutrition and domestic violence.
answer_hinglish: Loan chukaane ki zimmedari kisi ek ki nahi, group ki hai, aur kisi sadasya ke na chukaane pe baaki sadasya gambhirta se peecha karte hain, isliye banks bina collateral bhi udhaar dete hain. Is tarah SHGs collateral ki kami door karte hain aur samay pe uchit interest pe loan dilaate hain. Yeh grameen gareebon ke sangathan ki neev hain, mahilaon ko aarthik roop se aatmanirbhar banate hain, aur niyamit baithakein sehat, poshan aur gharelu hinsa jaise samajik muddon pe charcha ka manch deti hain.
ncert_context: Most of the important decisions regarding the savings and loan activities are taken by the group members. The group decides as regards the loans to be granted — the purpose, amount, interest to be charged, repayment schedule etc. Also, it is the group which is responsible for the repayment of the loan. Any case of non-repayment of loan by any one member is followed up seriously by other members in the group. Because of this feature, banks are willing to lend to the poor women when organised in SHGs, even though they have no collateral as such. Thus, the SHGs help borrowers overcome the problem of lack of collateral. They can get timely loans at a reasonable interest rate. Moreover, SHGs are the building blocks of organisation of the rural poor. Not only does it help women to become financially self-reliant, the regular meetings of the group provide a platform to discuss and act on social issues such as health, nutrition, domestic violence, etc.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Why are the poor unable to get bank loans, while moneylenders lend to them?
question_hinglish: Gareeb log bank loan kyun nahi le paate, jabki moneylenders unhe udhaar dete hain?
answer_english: Banks are not present everywhere in rural India, and even where present, bank loans require proper documents and collateral; absence of collateral is a major reason the poor cannot get them. Moneylenders know borrowers personally and lend without collateral, even before earlier loans are repaid, but they charge very high interest, keep no records and harass poor borrowers.
answer_hinglish: Gaon mein har jagah banks nahi hain, aur jahan hain wahan bhi loan ke liye sahi documents aur collateral chahiye; collateral na hona gareebon ko loan na milne ka bada kaaran hai. Moneylenders lene walon ko nijee roop se jaante hain aur bina collateral, purana loan chukne se pehle bhi, udhaar dete hain, par bahut zyada interest lete hain, record nahi rakhte aur gareebon ko pareshaan karte hain.
ncert_context: Poor households are still dependent on informal sources of credit. Banks are not present everywhere in rural India. Even when they are present, getting a loan from a bank is much more difficult than taking a loan from informal sources. Bank loans require proper documents and collateral. Absence of collateral is one of the major reasons which prevents the poor from getting bank loans. Informal lenders such as moneylenders, on the other hand, know the borrowers personally and hence are often willing to give a loan without collateral. The borrowers can, if necessary, approach the moneylenders even without repaying their earlier loans. However, the moneylenders charge very high rates of interest, keep no records of the transactions and harass the poor borrowers.

question_english: What was the main channel connecting countries in the past? How is it different now?

subject: Social Science
question_english: What are the various ways in which MNCs set up, control or produce in other countries?
question_hinglish: MNCs doosre deshon mein kin-kin tareekon se utpaadan lagaati, control karti ya karti hain?
answer_english: MNCs set up their own factories and offices; they set up production jointly with local companies, providing money for new machines and the latest technology; most commonly, they buy up local companies and expand production, like Cargill buying Parakh Foods; and they place orders with small producers in industries like garments, footwear and sports items and sell the products under their own brand names, controlling price, quality, delivery and labour conditions.
answer_hinglish: MNCs apni factory aur office lagaati hain; local companies ke saath milkar utpaadan karti hain, nayi machines aur latest technology ke liye paisa deti hain; sabse aam tareeka hai local companies khareed kar utpaadan badhana, jaise Cargill ne Parakh Foods khareedi; aur kapde, joote aur khel ke saamaan jaise udyogon mein chhote utpaadakon ko order dekar maal apne brand naam se bechti hain, daam, quality, delivery aur mazdoori ki shartein khud tay karti hain.
ncert_context: MNCs set up factories and offices for production. At times, MNCs set up production jointly with some of the local companies; the benefit to the local company is two-fold: MNCs can provide money for additional investments, like buying new machines for faster production, and might bring with them the latest technology. But the most common route for MNC investments is to buy up local companies and then to expand production. Cargill Foods, a very large American MNC, has bought over smaller Indian companies such as Parakh Foods. There's another way in which MNCs control production. Large MNCs in developed countries place orders for production with small producers. Garments, footwear, sports items are examples. The products are supplied to the MNCs, which then sell these under their own brand names. These large MNCs have tremendous power to determine price, quality, delivery, and labour conditions for these distant producers.

question_english: By 2017, Ford Motors sold 88,000 cars in India and exported 1,81,000 cars from India. What was its total output from India, and what share was exported?

subject: Social Science
question_english: What is the basic function of foreign trade?
question_hinglish: Foreign trade ka mool kaam kya hai?
answer_english: Foreign trade creates an opportunity for producers to reach beyond domestic markets, the markets of their own countries; they can sell within the country and also compete in markets of other countries. For buyers, importing goods produced in another country expands the choice of goods beyond what is domestically produced.
answer_hinglish: Foreign trade utpaadakon ko apne desh ke bazaar se aage pahunchne ka mauka deta hai; woh desh ke andar bhi bech sakte hain aur doosre deshon ke bazaaron mein bhi muqaabla kar sakte hain. Khareedaaron ke liye doosre desh mein bana saamaan mangaana desh mein bane saamaan se aage vikalp badhata hai.
ncert_context: For a long time foreign trade has been the main channel connecting countries. Trade routes connected India and South Asia to markets both in the East and West, and trading interests attracted companies such as the East India Company to India. To put it simply, foreign trade creates an opportunity for the producers to reach beyond the domestic markets, i.e., markets of their own countries. Producers can sell their produce not only in markets located within the country but can also compete in markets located in other countries of the world. Similarly, for the buyers, import of goods produced in another country is one way of expanding the choice of goods beyond what is domestically produced.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Explain with the example of Chinese toys how foreign trade leads to integration of markets.
question_hinglish: Chinese khilaunon ke example se samjhao ki foreign trade se bazaaron ka integration kaise hota hai.
answer_english: Chinese manufacturers began exporting plastic toys to India, where toys sold at high prices. With cheaper prices and new designs, Chinese toys became popular, and within a year 70 to 80 per cent of toy shops replaced Indian toys with Chinese ones. Indian buyers got more choice at lower prices, Chinese makers expanded business, but Indian toy makers faced losses. subject: Social Science
question_english: What is globalisation?
question_hinglish: Globalisation kya hai?
answer_english: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. Greater foreign investment and greater foreign trade have led to greater integration of production and markets across countries, with more goods, services, investments and technology moving between countries. MNCs are playing a major role in this process.
answer_hinglish: Globalisation deshon ke beech tezi se judaav ya integration ki prakriya hai. MNCs is prakriya mein badi bhoomika nibha rahi hain.
ncert_context: In the past two to three decades, more and more MNCs have been looking for locations around the world which would be cheap for their production. Foreign investment by MNCs in these countries has been rising. At the same time, foreign trade between countries has been rising rapidly. A large part of the foreign trade is also controlled by MNCs. The result of greater foreign investment and greater foreign trade has been greater integration of production and markets across countries. Globalisation is this process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. MNCs are playing a major role in the globalisation process. More and more goods and services, investments and technology are moving between countries.

question_english: How has improvement in transportation technology stimulated globalisation?
question_hinglish: Transport technology mein sudhaar ne globalisation ko kaise badhaava diya?
answer_english: Over the past fifty years, improvements in transportation technology have made faster delivery of goods across long distances possible at lower costs. Goods are placed in containers that can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks, hugely reducing port handling costs and increasing the speed with which exports reach markets. The cost of air transport has also fallen, allowing much greater volumes of goods to be carried by airlines.

Hawai transport bhi sasta hua, jisse airlines bahut zyada maal le jaane lagi.

subject: Social Science
question_english: What is a trade barrier? Give an example.
question_hinglish: Trade barrier kya hai? Ek example do.
answer_english: A trade barrier is a restriction set up by the government on foreign trade. Tax on imports is an example: if the government taxes imported toys, buyers pay a higher price, Chinese toys are no longer as cheap, imports fall and Indian toy-makers prosper. Governments use trade barriers to regulate foreign trade and decide what kinds of goods, and how much of each, should come into the country.
answer_hinglish: Trade barrier sarkar dwara foreign trade pe lagaayi gayi paabandi hai. Import pe tax iska example hai: agar sarkar imported khilaunon pe tax lagaaye, toh khareedaar zyada daam denge, Chinese khilaune utne saste nahi rahenge, import ghatega aur Indian khilauna banane wale tarakki karenge. Sarkar trade barriers se foreign trade niyantrit karti hai aur tay karti hai ki kaun sa aur kitna saamaan desh mein aaye.
ncert_context: Suppose the Indian government puts a tax on import of toys. Those who wish to import these toys would have to pay tax on this. Because of the tax, buyers will have to pay a higher price on imported toys. Chinese toys will no longer be as cheap in the Indian markets and imports from China will automatically reduce. Indian toy-makers will prosper. Tax on imports is an example of trade barrier. It is called a barrier because some restriction has been set up. Governments can use trade barriers to increase or decrease (regulate) foreign trade and to decide what kinds of goods and how much of each, should come into the country.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Why did the Indian government put barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment after Independence, and why did it remove them?
question_hinglish: Aazaadi ke baad Indian sarkar ne foreign trade aur foreign investment pe paabandiyan kyun lagaayi, aur unhe kyun hataaya?
answer_english: After Independence, barriers were considered necessary to protect producers within the country from foreign competition. Industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s, and import competition would not have let them grow, so only essential items like machinery, fertilisers and petroleum were imported. Starting around 1991, the government decided Indian producers should compete globally, believing competition would improve their quality; this was supported by powerful international organisations, so barriers were largely removed.
answer_hinglish: Aazaadi ke baad desh ke utpaadakon ko videshi muqaable se bachaane ke liye paabandiyan zaroori maani gayi. 1950s aur 1960s mein udyog bas shuru ho rahe the, aur import ka muqaabla unhe badhne nahi deta, isliye sirf machinery, khaad aur petroleum jaisi zaroori cheezein import hoti thi. Lagbhag 1991 se sarkar ne tay kiya ki Indian utpaadakon ko duniya se muqaabla karna chahiye, kyunki muqaable se unki quality sudhregi; taakatvar antarrashtriya sansthaon ke samarthan se paabandiyan kaafi had tak hataayi gayi.
ncert_context: The Indian government, after Independence, had put barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment. This was considered necessary to protect the producers within the country from foreign competition. Industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s, and competition from imports at that stage would not have allowed these industries to come up. Thus, India allowed imports of only essential items such as machinery, fertilisers, petroleum etc. Note that all developed countries, during the early stages of development, have given protection to domestic producers. Starting around 1991, some far-reaching changes in policy were made in India. The government decided that the time had come for Indian producers to compete with producers around the globe. It felt that competition would improve the performance of producers within the country since they would have to improve their quality. This decision was supported by powerful international organisations. Thus, barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment were removed to a large extent.

subject: Social Science
question_english: What is liberalisation of foreign trade?
question_hinglish: Foreign trade ka liberalisation kya hai?
answer_english: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is known as liberalisation. With liberalisation of trade, businesses can freely decide what they wish to import or export, goods can be imported and exported easily, and foreign companies can set up factories and offices. The government imposes much less restriction than before and is therefore said to be more liberal.

Sarkar pehle se bahut kam paabandiyan lagaati hai, isliye use zyada liberal kaha jaata hai.

subject: Social Science
question_english: What are quotas? How can they be used as trade barriers, using the example of Chinese toys?
question_hinglish: Quotas kya hain? Chinese khilaunon ke example se batao ki inhe trade barrier ki tarah kaise use kiya ja sakta hai.
answer_english: A quota is a limit placed by the government on the number of goods that can be imported. If the government sets a quota on Chinese toys, only a limited number can enter India, even if they are cheaper. This reduces competition for Indian toy-makers and protects them, much like a tax on imports, but limits buyers' choice.

subject: Social Science
question_english: Is trade under the WTO free and fair? Explain with the example of agriculture.
question_hinglish: Kya WTO ke tahat vyapaar free aur fair hai? Kheti ke example se samjhao.
answer_english: Not in practice. Developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers while WTO rules have forced developing countries to remove theirs. In India, agriculture provides the bulk of employment and a significant share of GDP, but in the US agriculture is just 1 per cent of GDP and 0.5 per cent of employment. Yet US farmers receive massive government payments, letting them sell surplus farm products in other countries at abnormally low prices, hurting farmers there. Developing countries ask whether this is free and fair trade.
answer_hinglish: Asal mein nahi. Viksit deshon ne galat tareeke se apni paabandiyan rakhi hain jabki WTO niyamon ne developing deshon ko paabandiyan hataane pe majboor kiya. India mein kheti zyadatar rozgaar aur GDP ka bada hissa deti hai, par US mein kheti GDP ka sirf 1 percent aur rozgaar ka 0.5 percent hai. Phir bhi US ke kisaanon ko sarkar se bahut paisa milta hai, jisse woh faltu fasal doosre deshon mein bahut saste mein bechte hain aur wahan ke kisaanon ko nuksaan hota hai. Developing desh poochte hain ki kya yeh free aur fair trade hai.
ncert_context: Though WTO is supposed to allow free trade for all, in practice, it is seen that the developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers. On the other hand, WTO rules have forced the developing countries to remove trade barriers. An example is the current debate on trade in agricultural products. The agriculture sector provides the bulk of employment and a significant portion of the GDP in India. Compare this to the US with the share of agriculture in GDP at 1% and its share in total employment a tiny 0.5%! And yet this very small percentage of people engaged in agriculture in the US receive massive sums of money from the US government for production and for exports. Due to this, US farmers can sell the farm products at abnormally low prices. The surplus farm products are sold in other country markets at low prices, adversely affecting farmers in these countries. Developing countries ask: 'You have asked our governments to stop supporting our farmers, but you are doing so yourselves. Is this free and fair trade?'

question_english: How has competition due to globalisation benefited people in India?
question_hinglish: Globalisation se aaye muqaable ne India ke logon ko kaise fayda pahunchaaya?
answer_english: Greater competition among local and foreign producers has benefited consumers, particularly the well-off in urban areas, who have greater choice, improved quality and lower prices, and enjoy higher living standards. MNCs have invested in cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and banking, creating new jobs, and local companies supplying raw materials to them have prospered. Kai badi Indian companies ne nayi technology mein investment kiya, standards badhaaye aur videshi companies ke saath sahyog se fayda uthaaya.

question_english: What are Special Economic Zones (SEZs), and what steps have governments taken to attract foreign investment?
question_hinglish: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) kya hain, aur sarkaron ne foreign investment aakarshit karne ke liye kya kadam uthaaye hain?
answer_english: SEZs are industrial zones set up by central and state governments with world-class facilities: electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, and recreational and educational facilities. Companies setting up units in SEZs pay no taxes for an initial five years. The government has also allowed flexibility in labour laws, letting companies hire workers 'flexibly' for short periods during intense work pressure, to reduce labour costs.

SEZs mein unit lagaane wali companies ko shuru ke paanch saal tax nahi dena padta. Sarkar ne labour laws mein bhi flexibility di hai, jisse companies kaam ke dabaav ke samay mazdooron ko kam samay ke liye 'flexibly' rakh sakti hain, taaki shram laagat ghate.
ncert_context: In recent years, the central and state governments in India are taking special steps to attract foreign companies to invest in India. Companies who set up production units in the SEZs do not have to pay taxes for an initial period of five years. Instead of hiring workers on a regular basis, companies hire workers 'flexibly' for short periods when there is intense pressure of work. This is done to reduce the cost of labour for the company. However, still not satisfied, foreign companies are demanding more flexibility in labour laws.

subject: Social Science
question_english: How was Ravi's capacitor unit in Hosur affected by rising competition after globalisation?
question_hinglish: Globalisation ke baad badhte muqaable se Hosur mein Ravi ki capacitor unit pe kya asar pada?
answer_english: Ravi started his capacitor company in Hosur, Tamil Nadu in 1992 with a bank loan and had 20 workers within three years. In 2001, the government removed restrictions on capacitor imports per its WTO agreement. Indian television companies, his main clients, were pushed by MNC brands into assembling for MNCs, and those still buying capacitors preferred imports at half Ravi's price. Ravi now produces less than half his 2000 output with only seven workers, and many friends in Hyderabad and Chennai closed their units.
answer_hinglish: Ravi ne 1992 mein bank loan lekar Hosur, Tamil Nadu mein capacitor company shuru ki aur teen saal mein 20 mazdoor ho gaye. 2001 mein sarkar ne WTO samjhaute ke tahat capacitor import pe paabandiyan hataayi. Uske mukhya graahak, Indian TV companies, MNC brands ke dabaav mein MNCs ke liye assembling karne lagi, aur jo capacitors khareedti thi woh Ravi ke aadhe daam pe import pasand karti thi. Ravi ab 2000 ke utpaadan se aadhe se kam banata hai aur sirf saat mazdoor hain, aur Hyderabad aur Chennai mein uske kai doston ki units band ho gayi.
ncert_context: Ravi took a loan from the bank to start his own company producing capacitors in 1992 in Hosur, an industrial town in Tamil Nadu. Capacitors are used in many electronic home appliances including tube lights, television etc. Within three years, he was able to expand production and had 20 workers working under him. His struggle to run his company started when the government removed restrictions on imports of capacitors as per its agreement at WTO in 2001. His main clients, the television companies, used to buy different components including capacitors in bulk for the manufacture of television sets. However, competition from the MNC brands forced the Indian television companies to move into assembling activities for MNCs. Even when some of them bought capacitors, they would prefer to import as the price of the imported item was half the price charged by people like Ravi. Ravi now produces less than half the capacitors that he produced in the year 2000 and has only seven workers working for him. Many of Ravi's friends in the same business in Hyderabad and Chennai have closed their units.

subject: Social Science
question_english: How has competition in the garment export industry affected workers, Indian exporters and foreign MNCs?
question_hinglish: Garment export udyog mein muqaable ne mazdooron, Indian exporters aur videshi MNCs ko kaise prabhaavit kiya?
answer_english: Large MNCs in Europe and America order garments from Indian exporters and look for the cheapest goods to maximise profits. To get these orders, exporters cut costs; since raw material costs cannot be reduced, they cut labour costs by hiring workers only temporarily. Workers face long hours, regular night shifts in peak season, low wages and forced overtime. The MNCs make large profits, while workers are denied their fair share of the benefits of globalisation.
answer_hinglish: Europe aur America ki badi MNCs Indian exporters se kapde mangaati hain aur zyada munaafe ke liye sabse sasta maal dhundhti hain. Order paane ke liye exporters laagat ghataate hain; kachche maal ki laagat nahi ghat sakti, isliye woh mazdooron ko sirf temporary rakh kar shram laagat ghataate hain. Mazdooron ko lambe ghante, peak season mein niyamit raat ki shift, kam vetan aur majboori ka overtime jhelna padta hai. MNCs bada munaafa kamaati hain, jabki mazdooron ko globalisation ke faydon ka uchit hissa nahi milta.
ncert_context: Large MNCs in the garment industry in Europe and America order their products from Indian exporters. These large MNCs with worldwide network look for the cheapest goods in order to maximise their profits. To get these large orders, Indian garment exporters try hard to cut their own costs. As cost of raw materials cannot be reduced, exporters try to cut labour costs. Where earlier a factory used to employ workers on a permanent basis, now they employ workers only on a temporary basis so that they do not have to pay workers for the whole year. Workers also have to put in very long working hours and work night shifts on a regular basis during the peak season. Wages are low and workers are forced to work overtime to make both ends meet. While this competition among the garment exporters has allowed the MNCs to make large profits, workers are denied their fair share of benefits brought about by globalisation.

subject: Social Science
question_english: How did globalisation change working conditions for Sushila, a garment worker in Delhi?
question_hinglish: Globalisation ne Delhi ki garment mazdoor Sushila ke kaam ki sthitiyon ko kaise badla?
answer_english: Sushila was a 'permanent worker' entitled to health insurance, provident fund and double-rate overtime until her factory closed in the late 1990s. After six months of searching, she got a job 30 km away, where even after several years she is a temporary worker earning less than half her earlier wage. She works seven days a week, from 7:30 a.m. to 10 p.m., gets no wage for a day off and has none of her earlier benefits.
answer_hinglish: Sushila ek 'permanent worker' thi jise health insurance, provident fund aur double rate pe overtime milta tha, jab tak 1990s ke ant mein uski factory band nahi hui. Chhe mahine dhundhne ke baad use 30 km door naukri mili, jahan kai saal baad bhi woh temporary mazdoor hai aur pehle se aadhe se kam kamaati hai. Woh hafte ke saato din subah 7:30 se raat 10 baje tak kaam karti hai, chhutti ke din ka vetan nahi milta aur pehle ka koi fayda nahi milta.
ncert_context: 35 year old Sushila has spent many years as a worker in garment export industry of Delhi. She was employed as a 'permanent worker' entitled to health insurance, provident fund, overtime at a double rate, when Sushila's factory closed in the late 1990s. After searching for a job for six months, she finally got a job 30 km. away from where she lives. Even after working in this factory for several years, she is a temporary worker and earns less than half of what she was earning earlier. Sushila leaves her house every morning, seven days a week at 7:30 a.m. and returns at 10 p.m. A day off from work means no wage. She has none of the benefits she used to get earlier. Factories closer to her home have widely fluctuating orders and therefore pay even less.
